{{Short description|Concept in linear algebra}}
In [[linear algebra]], a '''matrix pencil''' is a [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]]-valued function defined on a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>K</math>, usually the [[real numbers|real]] or [[complex numbers]].

== Definition ==
Let <math>K</math> be a field (typically, <math>K \in \{ \mathbb R, \mathbb C \}</math>; the definition can be generalized to [[rng (mathematics)|rngs]]<!-- this is NOT a typo -->, i.e. non-unital rings), and let <math>n > 0</math> be a positive integer. Then any matrix-valued function

:<math>P \colon K \to \mathrm{Mat}(K, n \times n)</math>

(where <math>\mathrm{Mat}(K, n \times n)</math> denotes the <math>K</math>-algebra of <math>n\times n</math> matrices over <math>K</math>) is called a '''matrix pencil.'''

=== Polynomial matrix pencils ===
An important special case arises when <math>P</math> is [[Polynomial function|polynomial]]: let <math>\ell \ge 0</math> be a non-negative integer, and let <math>A_0, A_1, \dots, A_\ell</math> be <math>n\times n</math> matrices (i. e. <math>A_i \in \mathrm{Mat}(K, n \times n)</math> for all <math>i = 0, \dots, \ell</math>). Then the '''polynomial matrix pencil''' (often simply a '''matrix pencil''') defined by <math>A_0, \dots, A_\ell</math> is the matrix-valued function <math>L \colon K \to \mathrm{Mat}(K, n \times n)</math> defined by

:<math>L(\lambda) = \sum_{i=0}^\ell \lambda^i A_i.</math>

The ''degree'' of this matrix pencil is defined as the largest integer <math>0 \le k \le \ell</math> such that <math>A_k \ne 0</math>, the <math>n \times n</math> [[zero matrix]] over <math>K</math>.

=== Linear matrix pencils ===
A particular case is a linear matrix pencil <math>L(\lambda) = A - \lambda B</math> (where <math>B \ne 0</math>).<ref>{{harvtxt|Golub|Van Loan|1996|p=375}}</ref> We denote it briefly with the notation <math>(A, B)</math>, and note that using the more general notation, <math>A_0 = A</math> and <math>A_1 = -B</math> (not <math>B</math>).

==Generalized eigenvalues of matrix pencils==
For a matrix pencil <math>P</math>, any <math>k \in K</math> such that <math>\det P(k) = 0_K</math> is called a '''generalized eigenvalue''' (often simply '''eigenvalue''') of <math>P</math>, and the set of generalized eigenvalues of <math>P</math> is called its '''spectrum''' and is denoted by

:<math>\sigma(P) = \{ k \in K : \det P(k) = 0_K \}.</math>

For a polynomial matrix pencil, we write <math>\sigma(A_0, \dots, A_\ell)</math>; for the linear pencil <math>(A, B)</math>, we write as <math>\sigma(A, B)</math> (not <math>\sigma(A, -B)</math>). 

The generalized eigenvalues of the linear matrix pencil <math>(A, I)</math> are precisely the matrix [[eigenvalue]]s of <math>A</math>. The general linear pencil <math>(A, B)</math> is said to have one or more eigenvalues ''at infinity'' if <math>B</math> has one or more 0 eigenvalues.

A pencil is called '''regular''' if there is at least one <math>k \in K</math> such that <math>\det P(k) \ne 0_K</math>, i. e. if <math>\sigma(P) \ne K</math>; otherwise it is called '''singular.'''

==Applications==
Matrix pencils play an important role in [[numerical linear algebra]]. The problem of finding the generalized eigenvalues of a pencil is called the [[generalized eigenvalue problem]]. The most popular [[algorithm]] for this task is the [[QZ algorithm]], an implicit version of the [[QR algorithm]] for solving the eigenvalue problem <math>Ax = \lambda Bx</math> without inverting the matrix <math>B</math> (which is impossible when <math>B</math> is singular, or numerically unstable when it is [[condition number|ill-conditioned]]).

==Pencils generated by commuting matrices==
If <math>AB = BA</math>, then the pencil generated by <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>:<ref>{{harvtxt|Marcus & Minc|1969|p=79}}</ref>

# consists only of matrices [[similar matrices|similar]] to a [[diagonal matrix]], or
# has no matrices in it similar to a diagonal matrix, or
# has exactly one matrix in it similar to a diagonal matrix.
